overview: This map entry covers early Soviet Ukraine in the 1920s, rather than a continuously independent Ukrainian republic. It became a founding republic of the USSR in 1922. Ukrainian-language education and cultural experimentation expanded during a decade that also brought famine, political control and increasing coercion.

periods.title: Early Soviet government
periods.summary: Soviet institutions consolidated while economic policy shifted in 1921.

periods.title: Within the new Soviet Union
periods.summary: The Ukrainian Soviet republic joined the USSR and promoted Ukrainian-language public life.

periods.title: A harsher turn
periods.summary: Stalin’s government dismantled the mixed economy and moved toward forced collectivization.

items.text: The New Economic Policy introduced in 1921 allowed a mixture of state ownership and limited private activity. Small businesses could operate, while heavy industry, banking and major transport remained state-controlled. Shopping and earning a living in the 1920s therefore differed from the later fully planned Soviet economy.

Farmers were allowed to sell produce after paying taxes, and could lease land or equipment. Cooperatives also expanded. These changes gave households more room to rebuild after war, although the authorities imposed heavier burdens and political restrictions on groups they considered opponents.

Famine devastated parts of Ukraine in 1921 through 1923. Drought and war damage combined with grain requisitions and the removal of food from the republic. Families struggled to obtain meals, and foreign relief organizations supplied food. Recovery was uneven and cannot be described simply as a successful economic restart.

A Soviet education system introduced in 1920 emphasized seven-year elementary schooling followed by technical training. It aimed to prepare industrial workers and address the needs of many homeless children. Lessons also carried political indoctrination, tying access to education closely to the government’s plans for society.

The 1920s literacy campaign taught adults as well as children, largely through Ukrainian. Wider reading and writing skills made newspapers, books and official documents accessible to more people. The same period’s Ukrainization policy expanded Ukrainian-language education and publishing, while remaining a policy of the Communist state.

Les Kurbas founded Berezil as an experimental theatre in Kyiv in 1922; it moved to Kharkiv in 1926. Its organization included actors’ studios, a directors’ laboratory, a design studio and a theatre museum. Making a performance was also a place for research and training.

Berezil actors trained in rhythm, movement and the use of props before concentrating on spoken language. Productions combined speech, gesture, music, lighting and visual design. An actor’s homework could involve learning to move convincingly before being allowed to deliver the big speech.

Kharkiv’s Derzhprom complex, constructed in the 1920s and completed in 1928, arranged large blocks around a square and linked them with bridges at different heights. Its dramatic shape expressed ambitions for a modern industrial capital. Office workers could move between parts of a building complex above street level.

A government decree in May 1928 established the Institute of Microbiology and Epidemiology in Kyiv. Its first director, Danylo Zabolotny, helped organize research into microorganisms and epidemic disease. This created a lasting scientific institution concerned with threats too small to see without laboratory tools.

A 1927 conference brought together scholars, teachers, journalists and writers to discuss Ukrainian spelling. Rules approved in 1928 were also adopted by scholarly organizations in 1929. Agreeing how words should be written helped education and publishing, but it required considerable discussion rather than a language simply inventing its own rulebook.

Surviving museum collections include magazines devoted to music, village theatre and rural women, alongside broader literary journals. Examples include Muzyka from 1925 and Silskyi teatr from 1928. These printed objects preserve the varied interests that readers could encounter during the decade.

Ukrainian Cyrillic on the title page of the 1929 first edition of the spelling rules: “УКРАЇНСЬКИЙ ПРАВОПИС”. Translation: “Ukrainian Orthography”, or rules for writing Ukrainian. The electronic reproduction identifies the State Publishing House of Ukraine; the rules themselves had been approved in 1928.

ending.text: The Ukrainian Soviet republic became part of the USSR in 1922 and continued beyond the map’s 1930 endpoint. The decade’s cultural and economic openings narrowed under Stalin; forced collectivization and repression led into a much harsher period. The map boundary marks coverage, not the disappearance of Ukraine.
